claims.text: The starting material is a monolithic CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix.
A physical-vapor-deposited adaptive coating can transition from a metallic state at low temperature to an oxide state at high temperature.
The coating will remain a robust, low-friction metallic interface at room temperature.
During elevated-temperature sliding, the coating will oxidize in a controlled manner.
Controlled oxidation will produce a continuous lubricious spinel layer at temperatures up to 800 °C.
The metallic low-temperature interface will lower friction at room temperature.
The high-temperature spinel layer will minimize both friction and wear.
The temperature-dependent transformation decouples the low- and high-temperature tribological requirements.
Relative to pristine CoCrFeNi, the coated alloy will have a significantly lower coefficient of friction throughout approximately 25–800 °C.
Relative to pristine CoCrFeNi, the coated alloy will have a reduced wear rate throughout approximately 25–800 °C.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi typically exhibits increasing friction at elevated temperature because of lattice disorder and uncontrolled surface oxidation.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi typically exhibits increasing wear at elevated temperature because of lattice disorder and uncontrolled surface oxidation.
The coating will be effective under moderate sliding loads in oxidizing environments from room temperature to 800 °C.
The coating may be less effective under extreme loads or highly reducing environments.
Thermal cycling may reduce effectiveness by causing coating delamination.
